title: Memorial Video Audio Restoration: Channel Fix, Noise Removal, and Dialogue/Music Balance in Ableton + iZotope RX
goal: Clean, repair, and balance the audio for a video containing dialogue and music, correcting the left/right channel imbalance without introducing phase problems and reducing unwanted noises while preserving the natural outdoor ambience of the recording.
context:
I am working on the audio for a video containing dialogue, music, and sound recorded outdoors. The recording has an imbalance between the left and right channels that needs to be corrected without introducing phase problems or damaging the spatial character of the original recording. The audio also contains unwanted noises and proximity effect sounds (low rumbles from the mic being too close) that need to be reduced or removed, while preserving enough natural outdoor ambience for the recording to continue sounding like it was recorded on location.

I will perform the audio editing, restoration, and mixing myself using Ableton Live and iZotope RX. I will use AI throughout the process to help evaluate possible approaches, troubleshoot specific problems, suggest restoration techniques, and develop solutions that preserve the character of the original recording.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not:
Yes, more or less. I would have probably done another quality check and made sure to line the video back up and make sure that version was clean, but I got a fairly good cut of the song itself from the recording.
Claude definitely helped, but also still slowed me a little.

Step 1.step_name: Assess the recording and Develop a Restoration Strategy
Step 1.step_action: I will listen through the complete recording and identify problems involving channel balance, dialogue clarity, music balance, unwanted noises, and environmental sound. I will describe the recording and the problems I hear to AI and use its recommendations to develop an appropriate order of operations before making significant changes to the audio.

nodes.label: Begin composing and describe the panning and proximity-effect problem to Claude
nodes.detail: With an idle Claude.ai home tab ("Back at it, Participant MinnesotaNLP") open alongside the Zoom troubleshooting window, the participant starts typing the description of the audio problem into a new chat, finishing the message just as the recording setup issue is resolved. In the new chat titled "Fixing panned guitar and vocal audio", the participant tells Claude that the source video (a man playing guitar, singing, and talking outdoors) has audio completely panned left, and asks for help addressing the stereo image, proximity effect, and general outdoor noise reduction.

nodes.label: Diagnose the routing cause and outline a general strategy
nodes.detail: After about 42 seconds of visible extended thinking, Claude explains the hard-left audio is almost certainly a mono mic fed into one channel of a stereo interface and mapped straight to left output -- a routing issue, not a signal problem -- and that this must be fixed before any EQ or noise reduction. It also flags that a static EQ cut is the wrong tool for proximity effect since it varies between singing and talking.

nodes.label: Check the video and open Ableton Live
Specify Ableton Live as the editing DAW
nodes.detail: The participant replies 'I'm using Ableton' so Claude can give exact device names and settings instead of generic advice.

nodes.label: Lay out a six-step Ableton processing chain
nodes.detail: Claude recommends, top to bottom: (1) Utility with Channel Mode set to 'Left' to center the signal, (2) EQ Eight high-pass at 80-100Hz, (3) Multiband Dynamics for proximity effect (downward compression confined to the 250-300Hz band), (4) a third-party denoiser since Ableton has no stock spectral denoiser (iZotope RX De-noise or Waves Clarity Vx), (5) an EQ automation lane for wind gusts, and (6) a 2:1-3:1 compressor plus De-Esser and a light closing EQ pass. It also flags a checkpoint: confirm the Utility 'Left' fix doesn't just relocate a pre-existing phase/comb-filter problem.

nodes.label: Set up the Ableton Live session and note the clipping
nodes.detail: While Claude generates its processing chain, he sets up the Ableton Live session with the song on a track, remarks that you can see the clipping in the waveform, and then moves on to prompt Claude.

nodes.label: Take a look at Claude's six-step Ableton processing chain

Step 2.step_name: Diagnose and Correct the Left/Right Channel Imbalance
Step 2.step_action: I will investigate the cause of the imbalance between the left and right channels, including differences in level, timing, frequency content, or other characteristics between the channels. I will use AI to help determine an appropriate method for correcting the imbalance while monitoring phase relationships and avoiding processing that causes comb filtering, cancellation, or other unwanted artifacts.

nodes.label: Add and configure the Utility device
nodes.detail: The participant searches the Ableton device browser for Utility, adds it to the AlbertoEmigrantSong audio track, and sets Channel Mode to Left, implementing Claude’s Step 1 recommendation to center the mono-sourced signal.

nodes.label: Ask Claude whether bouncing will lose the reference video
nodes.detail: The participant asks 'when I bounce after correcting stereo, I lose the video?', thinking through the workflow implications of exporting before doing heavier processing.

nodes.label: Explain Ableton's audio-only bounce and offer a video-remux fix
nodes.detail: Claude confirms Live's bounce/export is audio-only -- the loaded video is just a reference window -- and offers two fixes: a lossless ffmpeg remux command (`-map 0:v -map 1:a -c:v copy -c:a aac`) to swap the corrected audio onto the original video, or re-importing the bounced WAV into an NLE and syncing by a transient.

nodes.label: Decide to finish in Final Cut Pro instead of remuxing with ffmpeg
nodes.detail: Reads Claude's two options for putting the corrected audio back on the video. He skips the ffmpeg remux, saying he is not going to get that fancy, and chooses the simpler editor route, saying he will just use Final Cut Pro at the end.

nodes.label: Reveal the bounced file in Finder and apply RX noise reduction
nodes.detail: Opens the bounced 'AlbertoEmigrantSong' file in Finder, renames it, and opens it in iZotope RX. He samples a moment of silence, applies a light noise reduction so it still sounds outdoors, then rereads Claude's plan and confirms the high-pass and dynamic EQ were already done.

Step 3.step_name: Remove Distracting Noises While Preserving Outdoor Ambience
Step 3.step_action: I will identify distracting noises that interfere with the dialogue, music, or overall presentation and use iZotope RX or manual editing to reduce or remove them. I will use AI to help choose appropriate restoration methods while distinguishing between undesirable artifacts and natural environmental sounds that contribute to the sense of an outdoor recording.

nodes.label: Add gain reduction for headroom after De-clip
nodes.detail: Hears that the file is still clipping after De-clip, so he lowers the level a bit to get headroom, then judges that it sounds good.

nodes.label: Set a Pro-Q 3 dynamic EQ on the low mids and recheck Claude's list
nodes.detail: Opens FabFilter Pro-Q 3 and pulls down the 150-300 Hz range (about 3 dB around 200 Hz), the male-voice dynamic EQ Claude suggested for proximity effect. He rereads Claude's advice on wind and conservative noise reduction, says he already did those, then bounces in place to keep a copy.

nodes.label: Clean distracting noises by hand with RX Spectral Repair
nodes.detail: Opens the bounced file in RX and selects noisy patches with the wand tool. He uses Spectral Repair in attenuate mode (around 6 dB) and sometimes replace mode, checks the result, and backs off when it starts removing too many frequencies.

Step 4.step_name: Balance and Treat the Dialogue and Music
Step 4.step_action: I will balance the dialogue and music so that speech remains clear and intelligible while the music retains its intended presence and impact. I will use AI to help troubleshoot problems involving level, EQ, dynamics, masking, stereo image, and transitions between dialogue and musical material.

nodes.label: Ask Claude about overlapping chatter and mic movement at the song's intro
nodes.detail: The participant asks 'there seems to be a lot going on during the beginning of the song, it's kind of like the people talking over and the moving of the mic are getting in the way. What should I do?', flagging two stacked problems at the intro.

nodes.label: Distinguish the crosstalk problem from the mic-handling problem
nodes.detail: Claude explains that overlapping human chatter is fundamentally different from noise reduction -- a spectral denoiser can't separate two equally 'voice-shaped' sources, so expectations should be managed there -- while mic-movement bumps and handling thumps are short transient events that respond well to being fixed individually. It gives a five-card plan: isolate the intro as its own section, spot-treat the handling noise with RX Spectral Repair (or De-rustle), be realistic about the overlapping voices (Dialogue Isolate, or trim or fade), automate levels through the movement, and decide how much to keep as texture. It also recommends watching the intro back with picture first.

nodes.label: Review Claude's plan, then manually clean the intro in RX
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's reply and agrees that overlapping voices on one mono mic can't be cleanly separated and that the intro should be isolated as its own section. He then works through the noisy intro by hand on the RX spectrogram: he attenuates the worst patches, tries De-clip and a decrackle pass, runs De-click with the 'Multi-band (periodic clicks)' algorithm (Sensitivity 3.3, Frequency skew 3.5, Click widening 1.3ms, 35 clicks repaired) just in case, then finishes with a very light Spectral Repair attenuation (around 0.2). He says he is not going to use Music Rebalance, pulls down some low frequencies, and says the intro sounds pretty clean.
nodes.softwares: Claude (chat, claude.ai in Safari), iZotope RX 11 (Spectral Repair, De-clip, De-click)

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a mix/master plan for the isolated song section
nodes.detail: Having decided to cut just the song portion and mix/master it separately, the participant asks Claude for suggestions, noting the track is 'essentially a doubled mono signal at this point' and proposing EQ and compression, including a ~7k boost 'for wider image'.

nodes.label: Correct the stereo-width misconception and propose a mix plan
nodes.detail: Claude corrects the idea that EQ can widen a truly doubled-mono signal (L=R means there is no side-channel information for width tools to act on) and explains that real width would require actual decorrelation (short modulated delay, chorus, or a mono widener). Its five-card plan includes gentle Glue bus compression, light harmonic saturation with Saturator, and an optional mono-compatible widener. It suggests that for this single-mic outdoor performance, steps 1-3 and 5 plus skipping artificial widening may read as more honest than added stereo effects.

nodes.label: Save the session under a new name
nodes.detail: While Claude is answering, he uses File, Save As to save the session.

nodes.label: Cut out the song and build an EQ and compression chain, then check it against Claude's plan
nodes.detail: The participant renames the file, cuts the clip down to just the song, and fades it in. Seeing peaks all over the place, he adds Pro-Q 3 and a compressor (Glue), uses EQ Eight to pull down harsh peaks, and tries a de-hum. He thinks about adding reverb but decides to do that later.
nodes.softwares: Ableton Live (Pro-Q 3, Glue Compressor, EQ Eight), Claude (chat, claude.ai in Safari)

nodes.label: Check his work against Claude's plan
nodes.detail: Reads Claude's mix plan and finds that its gentle high-pass around 40-60 Hz and its Glue compressor are exactly what he had already done.
nodes.softwares: Ableton Live, Claude (chat, claude.ai in Safari)

nodes.label: Ride the volume by hand, add a 7kHz boost, and freeze the track
nodes.detail: The participant manually changes volumes to even out the loudness, then adds a high-shelf boost around 7kHz, his own idea from his prompt, saying he just thinks it sounds nice. He does not add a widener. He freezes the track and says the volume is much more consistent.

nodes.label: Reduce hum and leftover artifacts in RX
nodes.detail: The participant opens the frozen track in iZotope RX, runs de-hum because he still hears a lot of hum, then finds it too thin and switches to Spectral Repair in replace mode to fix leftover artifacts. He previews again and considers running de-hum a second time before going back to Finder.
nodes.softwares: Ableton Live, Finder, iZotope RX 11 (De-hum, Spectral Repair)

nodes.label: Add a last Pro-Q pass and browse EastWest Spaces II reverb presets
nodes.detail: The participant drags the repaired file back into Ableton, adds a balance control and Pro-Q 3 as the last step, then loads EastWest Spaces II and browses its presets (including studios and a guitar room he has used before) while deciding whether reverb suits an outdoor recording.

nodes.label: Ask Claude whether to use Inflator or reverb
nodes.detail: The participant asks 'should I use inflator or reverb?', weighing the harmonic-saturation option against the spatial option he was just browsing.

nodes.label: Explain the different purposes of Inflator and reverb
nodes.detail: Claude explains Inflator is a mono-compatible harmonic saturation/density tool that makes a recording feel bigger without touching the stereo image, while reverb adds real space and can legitimately widen a doubled-mono signal via differing L/R reflections -- but risks making the outdoor recording sound 'recorded indoors'. It recommends Inflator as the safer choice, with only a very subtle, short, low-mix reverb if used at all, and notes the two aren't mutually exclusive.

nodes.label: Read Claude's advice, then add Inflator, keep a light reverb, and export the audio
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's reply, then says he is 'cheating' by keeping some reverb, but it is only for this version of the recording, which is meant to be outdoors. He adds Inflator for saturation and keeps a light reverb, in line with Claude's point that the two are not mutually exclusive. He bounces, then exports the audio at 44.1 kHz, planning to combine it with the video later.
nodes.softwares: Claude (chat, claude.ai in Safari), Ableton Live (EW Spaces II, Inflator)

nodes.label: Ask Claude what loudness to target for the excerpted song
nodes.detail: The participant asks 'what loudness should I aim for with just the excerpted song?', thinking ahead to how the mastered clip will sit once remuxed back into the full video.

nodes.label: Recommend matching loudness to the surrounding dialogue sections
nodes.detail: Claude explains that since the song will likely be remuxed back into the full video, matching its loudness to the dialogue sections' measured level (using a metering plugin like the free Youlean Loudness Meter, since Ableton lacks a built-in one) matters more than hitting an exact LUFS figure in isolation; if the excerpt were to be released standalone instead, it suggests -14 LUFS integrated with a -1dB true-peak ceiling.

nodes.label: Read Claude's loudness advice and meter the output
nodes.detail: While Claude answers, he reads its advice, noting that it does not require matching and that -14 is the most, and lets the loudness meter analyze the main output.
nodes.softwares: iZotope RX 11, Claude (chat, claude.ai in Safari)

nodes.label: Set the loudness to -16, fix leftover clicks in RX, and export the WAV
nodes.detail: The participant checks the loudness with the loudness control and settles on -16, a little below Claude's -14. He fixes a few leftover artifacts in RX (replace mode, a click), then exports a WAV named 'Alberto emigrant song' with the date in his preferred format, and says he is done.
